title: Customer FW: DNS pinhole + TCP fallback intermittent control-plane failures (on-call notes)
content:
Summary:

On 2026-03-10 (UTC), multiple Private/VPC customers reported intermittent control-plane API timeouts and increased API latency from their on-prem agents to Redwood control endpoints. Impact lasted in waves for ~3 hours for affected customers, with error rates up to ~8% for control-plane RPCs originating from some customer networks.

High-level root cause (summary):
Customer firewalls with strict UDP fragment-dropping policies combined with large DNS responses (EDNS0 > 512 bytes) caused UDP DNS queries to fail. The customer edge devices blocked fragmented DNS UDP packets, and their firewall rules did not allow DNS TCP fallback (or blocked outbound TCP port 53). As a result, agents occasionally failed to resolve control-plane hostnames and fell back to cached IPs inconsistently; when DNS TTLs expired concurrently for many agents, a wave of failed DNS resolution produced transient loss of connectivity to control-plane endpoints.

Why this affected control plane specifically:
- Our agent resolves control-plane endpoints via customer resolvers (we rely on customer DNS for private deployments).
- EDNS0/glue records from some authoritative resolvers returned responses that exceeded 512 bytes (DNSSEC, additional records), requiring fragmentation or TCP fallback.
- Some firewalls are configured to drop fragmented UDP or to block TCP:53 to reduce attack surface.
- Without TCP fallback or successful UDP fragments, name resolution failed, so agents could not reach the control plane by name. Our internal retry/backoff combined with aggressive cache TTL expiry led to retries, increased latency, and eventual RPC failures.

Detection timeline (approx):
- 2026-03-10 01:04 UTC: Pager for elevated control-plane RPC error rate from customer cluster CUST-927 (alert: ctrlplane.rpc.errors > 5% sustained 5m).
- 2026-03-10 01:09 UTC: On-call (Aisha) triaged logs: agent logs show repeated "lookup \"control-01.redwood.internal\" failed: i/o timeout" entries.
- 2026-03-10 01:15 UTC: We triggered tcpdump on a customer-provided bastion (with permission) and observed repeated UDP DNS requests with no valid large-payload responses; repeated ICMP fragmentation-needed/fragmentation-lost from firewall.
- 2026-03-10 01:28 UTC: Customer confirmed their perimeter firewall policy had a rule: "drop fragmented UDP / drop dns-fragmentation" enabled as part of DDoS-hardening. They also had an outbound rule denying TCP/53 for non-approved hosts.
- 2026-03-10 01:36 UTC: Temporary mitigation applied: we pushed agent config to use our internal resolver proxy (TCP-based) for affected clusters and rolled an agent version that prefers TCP for DNS.
- 2026-03-10 03:45 UTC: Error rates dropped to baseline for impacted clusters. Ongoing: coordinated follow-up with customer to update firewall rules and their resolver settings.

Mitigation steps (what we did during the incident):
- Quick triage: checked agent logs for "lookup ... failed" messages and DNS lookup latency histogram in Console.
- Requested permission to run tcpdump on customer bastion/proxy to confirm packet-level drops. Commands used: tcpdump -n -s0 -w /tmp/dns.pcap udp port 53 and tcpdump -n -s0 -w /tmp/ctlplane.pcap host <control-ip>.
- Ran local dig queries from bastion: dig +noall +answer +bufsize=4096 control-01.redwood.internal @<cust-resolver> and dig +tcp control-01.redwood.internal @<cust-resolver> to demonstrate TCP succeeds and UDP fails.
- Temporarily updated agent configuration (agent remote-config) to set DNS fallback behavior: prefer TCP, lower EDNS buffer to 512, and increase DNS cache TTL to reduce queries during remediation. (PR#6723 contains the small agent patch.)
- Pushed a proxy route via our regional proxy (TCP TLS-based resolver) for affected customer to avoid using the customer resolver for control-plane hostnames until firewall rules were changed.
- Communicated with customer SRE/security team and requested they relax the "drop fragmented UDP" rule for their resolvers or explicitly allow DNS TCP outbound.

Root cause analysis (detailed):
- Contributing factors:
  - Some authoritative zones returned DNS responses >512 bytes (EDNS0) because of DNSSEC or additional records.
  - Customer perimeter device had a DDoS-hardening policy that dropped fragmented UDP packets (common for older appliances) and blocked outbound TCP/53 for non-admin hosts.
  - Our agent default behavior used system resolver with default EDNS size and relied on TCP fallback being allowed; we did not have robust detection for persistent UDP fragmentation failures.
  - TTLs for control-plane A/AAAA records were relatively short (60s) to enable fast failover/rollouts; this exacerbated the volume of DNS queries once failures started.

Why agent changes helped:
- Preferring TCP (or forcing TCP for DNS) avoids fragmentation issues because TCP carries the full response without fragmentation.
- Increasing the local DNS cache TTL reduced the query rate and smoke from repeated failed queries during the event.

Customer communication notes (snippet for PS/SE handoff):
- Short explanation: "Your firewall is dropping fragmented DNS UDP packets and blocking TCP fallback, causing our agents to intermittently fail to resolve control-plane hostnames."
- Recommended immediate actions for customer: allow outbound TCP port 53 for resolvers, and allow DNS fragments/fragmented UDP for responses between resolvers and their authoritative servers, or use a DNS forwarder that supports TCP/EDNS properly.
- Long-term: configure their resolver to perform TCP fallback or run a local forwarder. Where possible, add explicit allow rules for control-plane FQDNs during the maintenance window.

Runbook draft (for on-call) — Rapid checklist (short):
1) Confirm scope: check Console for clusters with elevated ctrlplane.rpc.errors and agent logs for "lookup failed" messages.
2) From allowed jump host/bastion, run:  dig +noall +answer +bufsize=4096 <control-fqdn> @<cust-resolver> and dig +tcp <control-fqdn> @<cust-resolver>. If TCP succeeds and UDP fails, that points to fragmentation/TCP-blocking.
3) Check for firewall/ACL rules: ask customer/network team for outbound TCP:53 deny or UDP-fragment-drop rules.
4) Collect packet capture: tcpdump -n -s0 -w /tmp/dns-frag.pcap host <resolver-ip> and look for UDP truncated responses or ICMP fragmentation-needed messages.
5) Apply mitigation: push agent config to prefer TCP DNS or route control-plane through our resolver proxy for affected clusters. Use rollouts with canary to limit blast radius.
6) Monitor: ensure RPC error rate returns to baseline and verify TTL expiry behaviour.
7) Follow up with customer: ensure firewall/config fixes and schedule a test window.

Commands/checks to include in runbook: (raw snippets for on-call)
- Check agent errors: grep -n "lookup .* failed" /var/log/redwood-agent.log | tail -n 100
- Local DNS checks: dig +noall +answer +bufsize=4096 control-01.redwood.internal @<cust-resolver>
- Force TCP: dig +tcp control-01.redwood.internal @<cust-resolver>
- Packet capture: sudo tcpdump -nn -s0 -w /tmp/dns.pcap udp port 53 or sudo tcpdump -nn -s0 -w /tmp/frag.pcap 'host <resolver-ip> and (udp port 53 or icmp)'
- Validate agent config: redwood-agentctl config get | grep dns

Follow-ups / action items (owner / ETA):
- (Aisha) Finalize and publish runbook entry in Confluence: "private-deployments: DNS fragmentation & firewall guide" — ETA 2026-03-18.
- (Diego) Add agent feature flag to prefer TCP dns for control-plane hostnames, enableable per-customer — ETA 2026-03-20. Track in JIRA-INFRA-3412.
- (Maya) Outreach to customer security team for the affected account; coordinate firewall rule changes and test window.
- (Platform) Evaluate increasing default DNS cache TTL for agents in private deployments from 60s to 180s (opt-in) to reduce blast radius during resolver instability — decision due 2026-03-25.
- (SRE) Instrument a new metric: "dns.resolve.failure_rate" broken down by resolver IP and TCP vs UDP resolution path. Add alert if UDP failure rate > 10% and TCP success > 80% to catch similar cases.

Notes to self / loose thoughts:
- Consider providing a small TCP-based resolver proxy as a managed option for private deployments where customer networks are unpredictable.
- We should document recommended firewall rule templates for common appliances (Palo Alto, Fortinet, Cisco ASA) covering DNS fragments and TCP/53.
- This pattern may repeat for other protocols that rely on large UDP payloads (e.g., some NTP/metrics aggregations) — add a "fragmentation" category to our incident taxonomy.

Attachments / evidence:
- packet captures (redacted) saved to S3: s3://redwood-evidence/CUST-927/dns-frag-20260310.pcap
- dig output snippets and agent log excerpts included in linked PR and Slack thread.

End of notes.

Status: draft postmortem / runbook fragment. Needs styling and transfer into Confluence.
